evidence.claim: Western Trails follows the North Platte valley between the Wyoming border and Ogallala, with rock formations and pine-shaded bluffs among the sights highlighted by Visit Nebraska.
evidence.quote: Pioneers would have come across the same towering formations and pine-shaded bluffs on this route as drivers encounter today.

evidence.claim: Nebraska DOT lists the scenic and historic byway as a 144-mile route along US 26 and Nebraska Highway 92.
evidence.quote: Western Trails Scenic & Historic Byway A 144-mile route from Ogallala northwest to the Wyoming border along U.S. Highway 26 and Nebraska Highway 92.

evidence.claim: US 26 largely parallels the river; east of Lewellen it crosses the water and passes through Ash Hollow.
evidence.quote: At Lewellen, US‑26 and N‑92 separate for the last time and shortly thereafter, US‑26 crosses the North Platte River again. After passing through Ash Hollow State Historical Park

evidence.claim: The modern highways parallel older journeys along the Oregon, California and Mormon trails.
evidence.quote: The highway also parallels the original paths of the Oregon, California, and Mormon trails.

evidence.claim: Highway 92 originally went through Mitchell Pass, then shifted to a more level route north of Scotts Bluff.
evidence.quote: Originally, Route 92 followed the route of the old Oregon Trail through Mitchell Pass in Scotts Bluff National Monument, and then through Downtown Gering. It was later rerouted on a more level route around the north side of Scotts Bluff, through the town of Scottsbluff.

evidence.claim: US 26 also changed course: its original alignment east of Lewellen lay north of the North Platte.
evidence.quote: From the creation of the highway in 1926 until the 1930s, US-26 went north of the North Platte River east of Lewellen.

evidence.claim: Lake McConaughy’s construction prompted the present alignment; the reservoir project was built between 1936 and 1941.
evidence.quote: When Lake McConaughy was built in the 1930s, the current alignment was constructed.

evidence.claim: the reservoir project was built between 1936 and 1941.
evidence.quote: it was constructed between 1936 and 1941 and is fed by the North Platte River.

evidence.claim: The gap between South Bluff and Scotts Bluff changed the emigrant route in 1851.
evidence.quote: Beginning in 1851, after the construction of a road between the bluffs, Mitchell Pass became the preferred route of the Great Platte River Road.

evidence.claim: Once a road had been built through it, travelers favored Mitchell Pass over Robidoux Pass because it shortened the journey and kept them closer to North Platte water.
evidence.quote: It was favored  over Robidoux Pass because it was both shorter and emigrants remained closer to the North Platte River, an important water source.

evidence.claim: The road’s builders are unknown.
evidence.quote: Who built the road through the pass about 1850 is unknown

evidence.claim: The Mormon Trail remained north of the river rather than using this gap.
evidence.quote: The northern branch of the Great Platte River Road, commonly called the Mormon Trail, did not use Mitchell Pass

evidence.claim: Pony Express riders and the first transcontinental telegraph also passed through.
evidence.quote: The Pony Express went through Mitchell Pass, as did the wires for the first transcontinental telegraph.

evidence.claim: Chimney Rock’s narrow pillar owes its survival to harder sandstone near the top, which protected it as the cliff line retreated south.
evidence.quote: The harder sandstone layers near the top have protected the pillar since it broke away from the retreating cliff line to the south.

evidence.claim: The formation consists mainly of Brule clay layered with volcanic ash and Arikaree sandstone.
evidence.quote: Chimney Rock consists primarily of Brule clay interlayered with volcanic ash and Arikaree sandstone.

evidence.claim: In the mid-19th century, it served as a landmark on the Oregon, California and Mormon trails, whose routes passed north of the rock.
evidence.quote: The formation served as a landmark along the Oregon, California, and Mormon Trails during the mid-19th century. The trails ran along the north side of the rock

evidence.claim: It remains visible to travelers on US 26 and Highway 92.

evidence.claim: The site received National Historic Site designation in 1956.

evidence.claim: Wagon ruts mark Windlass Hill, where the Oregon-California Trail descended from high tablelands into Ash Hollow and the North Platte valley.
evidence.quote: The hill marked the entrance from the high table lands to the south into the Ash Hollow area and the North Platte River valley. Wagon ruts are visible on the hill.

evidence.claim: The descent ran for about 300 feet at a 25-degree angle.
evidence.quote: Emigrants had a hard time going down the hill at a 25-degree angle, going down for about 300 feet.

evidence.claim: The name Windlass Hill came later; emigrants did not use it, and its origin is unknown.
evidence.quote: The name "Windlass Hill" was not used by the emigrants, and the source of the name is unknown.

evidence.claim: The state park also includes Ash Hollow Cave, 2.5 miles from the hill.
evidence.quote: The park comprises two attractions located 2.5 miles (4.0 km) from each other: Ash Hollow Cave and Windlass Hill.

evidence.claim: A nearby spring supported repeated habitation, and archaeological work identifies more than 1,500 years of Indigenous occupation.
evidence.quote: Archaeological explorations of the cave have revealed that at least four distinct indigenous cultures occupied this area, during a period of more than 1,500 years.
